definition: The user finds the service easy to enter but is obstructed when trying to leave, such as when cancelling a subscription.
source: Gray, Santos, Bielova & Mildner (2024). An Ontology of Dark Patterns Knowledge. CHI '24.

definition: The user is unable to resolve a help, cancellation, or complaint request because the pathway leads nowhere.
source: European Data Protection Board guidelines on dark patterns.

definition: The user is prevented from comparing the true cost-per-unit across differently packaged currency bundles.
source: Ofcom (2025). Persuasive Design Features and Potential Child Financial Harms (qualitative).

definition: The user cannot see the real-money cost of an item because it is obscured behind an intermediate virtual currency.
source: Gray, Santos, Bielova & Mildner (2024). An Ontology of Dark Patterns Knowledge. CHI '24.

definition: The user must complete multiple additional steps to deactivate purchase permissions or request a refund.
source: European Data Protection Board guidelines on dark patterns.

definition: The user is shown an advertised feature that turns out to require a purchase to actually access.
source: Brignull (2013) original dark patterns set.

definition: The user encounters advertising that is styled to look like game content or like a post from a trusted creator.
source: Brignull (2013) original dark patterns set.

definition: The user proceeds to checkout with optional purchases that were pre-selected on their behalf.
source: Brignull (2013) original dark patterns set.

definition: The user only discovers the real cost of a purchase at the final step of the transaction.
source: Brignull (2013) original dark patterns set.

definition: The user is shown an artificially inflated 'original' price that makes the discount appear larger than it is.
source: UK Competition and Markets Authority reports on online choice architecture.

definition: The user receives contradictory messaging across screens, such as 'free' shown prominently while fees appear in a footnote.
source: European Data Protection Board guidelines on dark patterns.

definition: The user is steered by the visual layout toward the paid or data-disclosing option.
source: UK Competition and Markets Authority reports on online choice architecture.

definition: The user sees the premium option displayed larger, brighter, or above the free alternative.
source: Gray, Santos, Bielova & Mildner (2024). An Ontology of Dark Patterns Knowledge. CHI '24.

definition: The users attention is drawn to a paid or more expensive option.
source: European Data Protection Board guidelines on dark patterns.

definition: The user is required to accept optional add-ons as an inseparable part of a single purchase.
source: UK Competition and Markets Authority reports on online choice architecture.

definition: The user is pushed with hard-sell prompts during moments of emotional engagement in gameplay.
source: Mathur et al. (2019). Dark Patterns at Scale. CSCW '19.

definition: The user finds spending limits, privacy permissions, or marketing opt-ins set permissively by default.
source: Bösch et al. (2016). Tales from the Dark Side: Privacy Dark Strategies.

definition: The user is shown celebratory effects, music, or character reactions that reinforce a purchase.
source: Gray, Santos, Bielova & Mildner (2024). An Ontology of Dark Patterns Knowledge. CHI '24.

definition: The user is presented with animated child-friendly characters that soften purchase prompts.
source: Luguri & Strahilevitz (2021). Shining a Light on Dark Patterns.

definition: The user sees declining framed as a social loss, such as 'Disappoint your team?'.
source: Gray, Santos, Bielova & Mildner (2024). An Ontology of Dark Patterns Knowledge. CHI '24.

definition: The user is asked a confusingly worded question where the default answer enables a purchase or data sharing.
source: Brignull (2013) original dark patterns set.

definition: The user is overwhelmed by an excessive number of purchase options at the point of decision.
source: European Data Protection Board guidelines on dark patterns.

definition: The user is left unaware of material facts about a purchase or data use because they are concealed in fine print or expandable sections.
source: Gray, Santos, Bielova & Mildner (2024). An Ontology of Dark Patterns Knowledge. CHI '24.

definition: The user is shown terms in language not appropriate to their age.
source: European Data Protection Board guidelines on dark patterns.

definition: The user is shown terms written in an adult legal register they cannot readily understand.
source: UK Competition and Markets Authority reports on online choice architecture.

definition: The user cannot tell what a button will do because its label does not clearly indicate the consequence.
source: European Data Protection Board guidelines on dark patterns.

definition: The user is repeatedly interrupted with purchase or upgrade prompts.
source: Gray, Santos, Bielova & Mildner (2024). An Ontology of Dark Patterns Knowledge. CHI '24.

definition: The user is enrolled in a free trial that automatically converts to a paid subscription without their explicit opt-in or reminder.
source: Brignull (2013) original dark patterns set.

definition: The user is recruited by friends who recieve rewards into purchases or new accounts.
source: Gray, Santos, Bielova & Mildner (2024). An Ontology of Dark Patterns Knowledge. CHI '24.

definition: The user finds their progression artificially gated behind payment.
source: US Federal Trade Commission reports on dark patterns.

definition: The user is required to invest excessive time unless they pay to skip ahead.
source: US Federal Trade Commission reports on dark patterns.

definition: The user is shown false or unverifiable scarcity messaging.
source: UK Competition and Markets Authority reports on online choice architecture.

definition: The user is shown indicators such as '247 people are looking at this right now'.
source: Mathur et al. (2019). Dark Patterns at Scale. CSCW '19.

definition: The user is shown indicators suggesting peer endorsement or purchase activity.
source: Mathur et al. (2019). Dark Patterns at Scale. CSCW '19.

definition: The user is shown 'Only 2 left' messaging that is often unverifiable.
source: Mathur et al. (2019). Dark Patterns at Scale. CSCW '19.

definition: The user is shown false or undisclosed paid endorsements styled as user-generated content.
source: Mathur et al. (2019). Dark Patterns at Scale. CSCW '19.

definition: The user is targeted by trusted creators promoting purchases or affiliate codes to them.
source: US Federal Trade Commission reports on dark patterns.

definition: The user is pressured by an 'Offer ends soon' message with no specified end time.
source: Mathur et al. (2019). Dark Patterns at Scale. CSCW '19.

definition: The user is shown a countdown such as 'Offer expires in 02:34:18' on a purchase prompt.
source: Mathur et al. (2019). Dark Patterns at Scale. CSCW '19.

definition: The user is shown 'Today only' promotions on in-app purchases.
source: Mathur et al. (2019). Dark Patterns at Scale. CSCW '19.

definition: The user is shown decline language designed to shame them, such as 'No thanks, I don't want to be the best'.
source: Brignull (2013) original dark patterns set.

definition: The user is shown prompts/ads behaviourally targeted to their observed behaviour patterns to induce spending.
source: UK Competition and Markets Authority reports on online choice architecture.

definition: The user pays for a randomised reward whose odds are concealed from them.
source: Zendle et al. (2019). Loot boxes are again linked to problem gambling.

definition: The user pays for pull-based randomised character or item draws.
source: Zendle et al. (2019). Loot boxes are again linked to problem gambling.

definition: The user is forced into a time-cost decision by artificial friction.
source: Fitton & Read (2019). Creating a Framework to Support the Critical Consideration of Dark Design Aspects in Free-to-Play Apps.

definition: The user interacts with a platform deliberately designed to visually resemble gambling.
source: Ofcom (2025). Persuasive Design Features and Potential Child Financial Harms (qualitative).

definition: The user is offered paid items that grant an in-game advantage over non-paying players.
source: Fitton & Read (2019). Creating a Framework to Support the Critical Consideration of Dark Design Aspects in Free-to-Play Apps.

definition: The user completes a purchase with reduced decision-point friction, in a single tap.
source: Ofcom (2025). Persuasive Design Features and Potential Child Financial Harms (qualitative).

definition: The user is anchored toward a bundle by a premium tier positioned against an artificially worse alternative.
source: Ofcom (2025). Persuasive Design Features and Potential Child Financial Harms (qualitative).

definition: The user is given a payment product whose default settings are configured to maximise spending capacity.
source: Information Commissioner's Office. Age-Appropriate Design Code (Children's Code).

definition: The user experiences game content that functions as advertising for products or brands.
source: OECD (2021). Children in the Digital Environment.

definition: The user is presented with a counterfeit login interface imitating a popular gaming or social platform.
source: Online Safety Act 2023.

definition: The user is contacted by a compromised peer account requesting a transfer of in-game currency or money.
source: Online Safety Act 2023.

definition: The user is offered a false promise of free currency that exploits their optimism.
source: OECD (2021). Children in the Digital Environment.

definition: The user is recruited as a financial intermediary under the guise of a legitimate earning opportunity.
source: Online Safety Act 2023.

definition: The user experiences a delay between spending and receiving an item, weakening their ability to link the action to its consequence.
source: Ofcom (2025). Persuasive Design Features and Potential Child Financial Harms (qualitative).

definition: The user is offered limitless item or skin upgrades.
source: Ofcom (2025). Persuasive Design Features and Potential Child Financial Harms (qualitative).

definition: The user is able to spend through mechanisms that bypass parental authorisation.
source: OECD (2021). Children in the Digital Environment.

definition: The user makes repeated small purchases that individually fall below the threshold at which loss is felt.
source: Ofcom (2025). Persuasive Design Features and Potential Child Financial Harms (qualitative).

definition: The user is groomed into high-value spending through targeted offers and identity-tied status.
source: Ofcom (2025). Persuasive Design Features and Potential Child Financial Harms (qualitative).

definition: The user pays in good faith for a physical or digital item that is never delivered, often on informal marketplaces with weak seller verification.
source: ParentZone A problem hiding in plain sight? Children spending, making and losing money online (Parentzone 2023)

definition: The user stakes earned or purchased in-game items on unregulated third-party gambling sites, which is illegal for under-18s in the UK.
source: ParentZone A problem hiding in plain sight? Children spending, making and losing money online (Parentzone 2023)

definition: The user is persuaded to invest savings, allowance, or borrowed money into a fraudulent or structurally losing cryptocurrency scheme.
source: ParentZone A problem hiding in plain sight? Children spending, making and losing money online (Parentzone 2023)

definition: The user, following an earlier loss, is contacted by someone claiming to help recover it who instead extracts further money or data.
source: ParentZone A problem hiding in plain sight? Children spending, making and losing money online (Parentzone 2023)

definition: The user is impersonated to their parent via SMS or messaging app to extract money, often without the user knowing the scam occurred.
source: ParentZone A problem hiding in plain sight? Children spending, making and losing money online (Parentzone 2023)

definition: The user is shown a list of component prices without being given the aggregated total.
source: Behavioural Insights Team. Review of Online choice and Vulnerability. (Citizens Advice, 2023(

definition: The user is induced to commit to a future behaviour, exploiting the psychological cost of breaking that commitment.
source: UK Competition and Markets Authority reports on online choice architecture.

definition: The user pays more as an existing customer than a new customer would for the same service, and must expend effort to switch.
source: UK Competition and Markets Authority reports on online choice architecture.

definition: The user is offered a frictionless deferred-payment option at checkout that separates the spending decision from the payment moment, despite under-18 credit restrictions.
source: UK Competition and Markets Authority reports on online choice architecture.

definition: The user is recruited through someone impersonating recruitment staff, paid a small sum to build trust, then asked for an upfront fee that is never refunded.
source: North Yorkshire Police (2025). Warning from North Yorkshire Police to parents and young people. September 2025

definition: The user has their trust in in-game trading exploited by a peer who steals items, currency, or account access with no platform compensation.
source: ParentZone A problem hiding in plain sight? Children spending, making and losing money online (Parentzone 2023)

definition: The user is promised free in-game currency in exchange for credentials, surveys, or downloads, but the currency never arrives and their account or device is compromised.
source: ParentZone A problem hiding in plain sight? Children spending, making and losing money online (Parentzone 2023)

definition: The user downloads modifications that instead contains malware compromising their device, credentials, or payment information.
source: Kaspersky (2024). 30 percent more young gamers targeted by cybercriminals in H1 2024 vs. H2 2023. Kaspersky press release, 5 September 2024.

definition: The user encounters an AI-cloned voice impersonating them to their parent, or impersonating a trusted figure to them, often alongside spoofed phone numbers.
source: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internet Crime Complaint Center (2026). 2025 Internet Crime Report. Federal Bureau of Investigation.

definition: The user is shown AI-generated video or audio of a celebrity appearing to endorse a scheme, and acts believing the endorsement is genuine.
source: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internet Crime Complaint Center (2026). 2025 Internet Crime Report. Federal Bureau of Investigation.

definition: The user buys or sells a gaming account outside the platform's terms, risking loss of the account, recovery by its original owner, or involvement in fraud.
source: ParentZone A problem hiding in plain sight? Children spending, making and losing money online (Parentzone 2023)

threat: Spatial Coercion in 3D and Immersive Environments
definition: The user encounters paid items or prompts placed in unavoidable 3D, VR, or AR paths, requiring effortful spatial action to dismiss.
source: [KFC — full reference missing from Coverage Key]

definition: The user's attention is deliberately drawn away from one interface element toward another, so they make a choice without registering the disfavoured option.
source: Brignull (2013) original dark patterns set.

definition: The user is shown a choice that appears to require a decision but has been silently pre-filled toward the designer's preferred outcome, and proceeds without registering it.
source: Gray, Santos, Bielova & Mildner (2024). An Ontology of Dark Patterns Knowledge. CHI '24.

definition: The user is faced by lengthy terms they had no realistic prospect of reading, even though the language itself is comprehensible.
source: Bösch et al. (2016). Tales from the Dark Side: Privacy Dark Strategies.

definition: The user is profile and the resulting profile is used to personalise persuasive commercial content that induces spending.
source: Bösch et al. (2016). Tales from the Dark Side: Privacy Dark Strategies.

definition: The user is given feedback such as sounds, animations, or score increments timed during purchase to reinforce their behaviour in an operant conditioning loop.
source: UK Competition and Markets Authority reports on online choice architecture.

definition: The user is shown information without structure, so key details are missed.
source: European Data Protection Board guidelines on dark patterns.

definition: The user has their account taken over after downloading cheat software losing access to any account credit.
source: [Mal24 — full reference missing from Coverage Key]

definition: The user purchases a product believing additional items or features are included, but important exclusions are concealed until after purchase.
source: Primary focus-group data (this study)

definition: The user is unable to reverse an unauthorised or regretted purchase because refund and chargeback pathways are obstructed, slow, or require proof the user cannot provide.
source: Primary focus-group data (this study)

definition: The user is directed to complete payment outside the game's official channels removing platform safeguards and making the transaction irreversible.
source: Brignull (2013) original dark patterns set.

definition: The user is coerced into transferring money or in-game currency under threat of exposure of intimate images.
source: Ofcom (2025). Persuasive Design Features and Potential Child Financial Harms (qualitative).

definition: The user is exposed to malware or a fraudulent site through a malicious advertisement.
source: Ofcom (2025). Persuasive Design Features and Potential Child Financial Harms (qualitative).

definition: The user buys or sells in-game currency or items for real money through unofficial third-party channels and unwitting involvement in money laundering.
source: Jensen & Kristiansen (2026) Victimization in online gaming-related trade scams: A study among young Danes
